subject: choosing the correct response family for a dsm

messages.author: 5e426c478a162ca8
messages.subject: choosing the correct response family for a dsm
parts:
Hi there, my name is Kevin Hawkshaw and I'm a PhD student at the University of Alberta. I'm working with a dsm modeling abundance for various avian and mammalian groups in an arctic system. I have a bit of an conundrum when it comes to deciding on a response family based on the diagnostic plots of gam.check. I've tried quasipoisson, Tweedie and negative binomial.

the qq plot for the quasipoisson distribution looks pretty bad, so i more or less ruled that one out. 
Tweedie response is quite good for the majority of the distribution on the qq plot, however there is evidence of overdispersion at the upper end of the distribution driven by maybe a dozen abnormally large segment counts, and these are not sampling errors. 
I then tried the negative binomial distribution, which does much better with the overdispersion, but develops this weird kink at the lower end of the distribution, which (if i have this right) is evidence of some unmodeled zero inflation.
i'm also concerned by the unusual looking histogram of residuals which looks more bimodal than normal. my dataset is decent sized (>1000 observations, >2000 segments), so there shouldn't be sample size issues. Can anyone offer some advice here? what is the lesser of these three evils? is there another response family that might fit my data better? happy to provide more information if I haven't done a good job explaining.

Thanks very much,
Kevin

messages.author: 5e426c478a162ca8
messages.subject: Re: choosing the correct response family for a dsm
parts: OK, so I've thought of one potential solution. I could increase the length of my transect segments (or use the entire transect) to reduce the degree of zero inflation. My surveys are multispecies, and for the species groups I am currently analyzing (songbirds and shorebirds) I am working with 250m transect segments, chosen because it is approximately double the truncation distance of my observation data (where detection < 15%), thus the segments are approximately square. The vast majority of my transects are ~ 1km long, so potentially using the entire transect could solve my response distribution problem, but I'm not sure how valid this is in density surface modeling. It would mean that for species groups with shorter truncation distances, the segments are not going to be square. How problematic would this be?

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Re: choosing the correct response family for a dsm
parts:
Hi Kevin, hi listfolk,

The squareness of the segments is by no means essential for the DSM approach to work. Things to bear in mind are:

- not having segments to short that you end up "binarising" your response (i.e., just 1s and 0s)
- not making segments so long that there is little information about spatial pattern
- enabling use of any spatial predictors at the resolution that would be meaningful (e.g., not averaging over SST such that there's so information to build a model)

Hope this helps!

cheers,
--dave
